## Oct 11 Results: The Cold, Hard Numbers

Let's not sugarcoat it—0-1 is 0-1. The Dodgers pick at 50% confidence didn't materialize, and when you're running at 0.0% accuracy, there's nowhere to hide in the data. But here's what the numbers actually tell us: a 50% probability pick is essentially a coin flip, and variance is part of the game.

## The Statistical Reality

When you make a 50% confidence pick, you're essentially saying the game is a toss-up. Missing on one doesn't invalidate the model—it's the expected outcome half the time. What matters is long-term accuracy across a statistically significant sample size. One game? That's noise, not signal.

## Oct 12 Preview: Running It Back

Here's where it gets interesting from an analytical standpoint: we're going right back to the same matchup. Dodgers at Brewers, Game 2. The probability model? Still sitting at 50%. The difference? Yoshinobu Yamamoto takes the mound for LA against Logan Henderson.

## The Pitcher Matchup By The Numbers

Yoshinobu Yamamoto brings electric stuff to the table—we're talking about a pitcher with elite spin rates and swing-and-miss capability. Logan Henderson is the less experienced arm here, which typically shows up in the underlying metrics. But here's the thing: in playoff baseball, traditional stats get compressed. Small sample size variance explodes. That's why we're still at 50% confidence.

## What The Model Sees

The 50% probability reflects what the data is telling us: this series is legitimately even. Home field advantage for Milwaukee offsets some of the Dodgers' talent edge. The pitching matchup favors LA on paper, but Henderson at home in a playoff environment creates uncertainty the model accounts for.

Bottom line: we're making the same pick because the underlying fundamentals haven't changed. Variance went against us on Oct 11. Let's see what the numbers say after Oct 12.
